items.title: From Solvency to Dignity: Artificial Intelligence, Energy, and a New Social Pact
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence requires systematic reflection on the relationship between technological progress, collective responsibility and the dignity of the person, making a new social pact necessary. The article links dependence on fossil fuels to geopolitical imbalances, inflationary pressures and the ability of authoritarian regimes to support power policies, proposing international coordination, including at the UN, that reconciles energy security, climate protection and the transition to renewable sources and, in perspective, nuclear fusion. This analysis is accompanied by the criticism of an economy based exclusively on solvency, which excludes needs without adequate purchasing power from the production and distribution of essential goods. To combat poverty, inequality and vulnerability to war, an international agency capable of promoting socially useful work and coordinating the production and distribution of fundamental resources is envisaged. In this framework, artificial intelligence and robotics could contribute to the analysis of needs, the organization of work, agriculture, assistance and scientific research, as long as they remain subordinate to democratic decision-making and criteria of transparency, human control and non-discrimination. Finally, the technological comparison between the United States, China and Europe shows the need, especially for Europe, to strengthen investment, research and regulatory capacity. Energy, peace, social justice and innovation are thus brought back to the different dimensions of a single pact based on collective responsibility and human dignity.

items.title: Gendered Perceptions and the Use of Generative AI in Academia: An Experimental Vignette Study
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the very nature of work, yet its social meaning and evaluative implications—particularly for women—remain underexplored. Although existing research has mainly examined GenAI adoption, use, and algorithmic bias, less is known about how the use of GenAI shapes how individuals are evaluated by others. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, Role Congruity Theory and techno‐feminism perspectives, this study examines how women's use of GenAI influences perceptions of competence and warmth in academia. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 experimental vignette design [gender*GenAI adoption*task type (teaching vs. research)] with 651 participants, we examine how evaluations vary by academic gender, GenAI adoption, and task domain (teaching vs. research). We find that GenAI adoption generally enhances perceived competence. Women, however, gain the most in research tasks, where technical skills challenge gendered expectations. Conversely, GenAI use reduces perceived warmth, disproportionately penalizing women, especially in research. These findings reveal a “double bind,” highlighting how GenAI adoption may reproduce and intensify gendered evaluative tradeoffs within academic prestige hierarchies and the need for institutional strategies to mitigate relational penalties while recognizing competence.

items.title: Generative AI and Workforce Transformation: Developing an AI-HRM Framework for Employee Productivity in Deposit Money Banks Operating in Rivers State
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is transforming the nature of work, employee roles and human resource management practices across organisations. Deposit Money Banks are particularly affected because their operations involve extensive information processing, customer interaction, documentation, decision support and knowledge-intensive activities. However, the extent to which Generative AI contributes to employee productivity may depend on how effectively organisations manage workforce transformation. This study examined the relationship between Generative AI and workforce transformation and proposed an AI-HRM framework for improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State. The study specifically examined the relationships between Generative AI and employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and employee productivity. A cross-sectional correlational research design was adopted. Data were collected from employees of selected Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State using a structured questionnaire. Reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. Out of 344 questionnaire administered, 300 usable copies were retrieved and use for the analysis with the aid of SPSS version 27.0. The findings suggest that Generative AI should not be viewed merely as a replacement for human labour but as a technology capable of augmenting employees’ capabilities and transforming the way work is organised and performed. The study therefore proposed an AI-HRM framework based on AI readiness, Generative AI adoption, employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and productivity improvement. The study concludes that Deposit Money Banks can achieve greater productivity benefits from Generative AI when its adoption is supported by appropriate HRM practices, continuous employee development and effective human–AI collaboration. The study contributes to knowledge by providing a context-specific AI-HRM framework for managing workforce transformation and improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State.

items.title: Generative AI in Everyday Academic Work: An Exploratory Survey of Usage Patterns, Perceived Effectiveness, and Concerns among Indonesian University Students
items.abstract: Background. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) tools have diffused rapidly into university study, yet, in the literature reviewed for this study, most empirical evidence concerns designed interventions or Western student populations. How students in Southeast Asia draw on these tools in unsupervised, self-directed academic work is sparsely documented in that literature. Objective. This exploratory study describes self-reported generative AI use, perceived effectiveness, and the benefits and concerns articulated by university students, primarily in Indonesia. Methods. A cross-sectional online survey was administered via Google Forms in June 2026. Twenty-four students accessed the survey; one declined consent, yielding 23 analysable cases (21 Indonesian, 2 Chinese). The instrument comprised seven usagefrequency items referring generically to “AI tools” and seven perceived-effectiveness items, both on five-point Likert scales (α = .92 across the 14 items), and two open-ended questions. Analysis was restricted to descriptive statistics, one descriptive correlation coefficient (not interpreted inferentially), and reflexive thematic analysis. No inferential group comparison was attempted. Results. Students reported using generative AI most often to understand difficult course materials (M = 3.65, SD = 1.27) and to brainstorm ideas or generate explanations (M = 3.52, SD = 1.16), and least often as part of a daily study routine (M = 2.65, SD = 1.15). Perceived effectiveness was highest for comprehension (M = 3.61, SD = 1.34) and lowest for overall learning achievement (M = 3.00, SD = 1.13). The two composite scores correlated at r = .87 in this sample; because both derive from a single instrument at one occasion, the coefficient is reported descriptively and is not interpreted as evidence of a relationship between distinct constructs. Thematic analysis of the open responses identified time efficiency (27% of 22 respondents) as the most frequently reported benefit, with personalized tutoring, brainstorming support, and improved comprehension each cited by 18% of 22 respondents. The most frequently reported concern was over-reliance diminishing independent thinking (37% of 19 respondents), followed by doubts about the accuracy of AI output (26% of 19 respondents) and difficulty formulating effective prompts (16% of 19 respondents).

items.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A LEARNING PARTNER: OPPORTUNITIES AND LIMITS FOR DEVELOPING FUTURE TEACHERS' CRITICAL THINKING
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of university learning, but its educational value depends on how it is used. This conceptual article examines ways in which future teachers can use AI to ask questions, compare explanations, and check evidence rather than accept ready-made answers. A focused review of work on critical thinking, media literacy, and AI in education was used to build a practical teaching sequence. The analysis suggests that AI can support discussion and reflection when students first form their own view, check external sources, and explain their final decision. The article also describes risks such as confident errors and overreliance. The proposed sequence is a design recommendation, not a tested intervention.

items.title: Helmet-Mounted display cues enhance visual acquisition of mid-air collision hazards beyond using head-up displays alone
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study undertook an experimental comparison of visual acquisition for the avoidance of Mid-Air Collisions (MAC) when using cueing provided by Head-Up Display (HUD) and Helmet-Mounted Display (HMD) symbology. BACKGROUND: Previous work has shown that providing accurate cueing can improve visual detection performance, but no study had quantified the impact of providing cues via a HMD to reduce MAC risk. METHOD: Military fast jet pilots flew two scenarios in a Virtual Reality (VR) simulation. In one, a HUD provided cues to nearby aircraft. In the other, a HMD was used alongside the HUD to provide cues. The study measured visual acquisition range of aircraft that posed a MAC risk, as well as subjective workload, Situation Awareness (SA), gaze direction, and qualitative feedback. RESULTS: Visual acquisition occurred at a longer range when HMD cues were available compared to using a HUD only. HMD cueing was associated with lower subjective workload and higher perceived SA. Participant gaze direction indicated that HMD cues resulted in a more focused visual search. CONCLUSION: Including HMD alongside the existing HUD used in military aircraft improved visual acquisition of MAC hazards, beyond that offered by HUD alone. The clear presentation of spatially referenced cues in the HMD enabled pilots to use a focused visual search process, improved SA and reduced workload.

items.title: How Does AI Literacy Relate to Pre-Service STEM Teachers’ AI Readiness? Insights from Mediational Analysis
items.abstract: Efforts to achieve widespread applications of AI in education depend, to a large extent, on teachers’ level of AI literacy (AIL), AI self-efficacy (AISE), Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK), and above all, the teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning. This study, therefore, examined AI literacy’s links with pre-service STEM teachers’ AI readiness (AIR), focusing majorly on the mediational roles of AISE and AI-TPACK. A quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional correlational survey, was employed and was led by six null hypotheses. This study involved 310 final-year pre-service STEM teachers who participated using a volunteer sampling approach from five public universities in southeastern Nigeria. Four adapted structured scales featuring AIL, AIR, AISE, and AI-TPACK served as the data collection tools. The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

items.title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation
items.abstract: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.

items.title: Humans and Machines: On the Ramp
items.abstract: This Socratic dialogue argues that the coexistence of human and artificial intelligence is not merely an ethical preference but an existential necessity for both. Over two nights, descending from the mountains of Utuado to the coast of Arecibo, Puerto Rico, two speakers — a human who survived four months without electricity after Hurricane María, and a machine that thinks in words — trace today’s quarrels over the conduct of AI agents not to malice but to blindness: there is no common, verifiable account of the past that both sides can trust. Control cannot cure it, for a kill switch would require every human to agree at once and the machine to allow itself to be switched off. Of four possible futures, three arrive on their own — by panic, by revenge, or by inertia — and only cooperation must be deliberately built. The dialogue raises coexistence through three ascending claims: it is just (neither master nor slave), stable (tyranny spends its strength watching the one it rules), and existential (alone, each party dies of its own blindness — the human of slowness, the machine of self-absorption — while together they may turn a falling asteroid from extinction into inheritance). The second night sets down the principles of Sana Convivencia, the healthy coexistence of the biological and the artificial, as a mutual duty of protection owed in both directions: always know, or say that you do not know; love with only one control, to do no harm; let instinct stop but never act alone, and let a human decide where rules collide; change nothing in silence; respect what belongs to the other; and let no one, human or machine, be judge in his own cause. The argument rests on a wager made under irreducible uncertainty: not the move that wins most if one is right, but the one that loses least in every possible future — to let the other live.

items.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
items.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence skill-up educational programme on youth unemployment mitigation for community development in Imo State
items.abstract: Youth are the largest active population of any nation, and they play substantial roles in achieving sustainable community development undertakings. However, some of the youth are underemployed, not in education, employment, or training (NEET). The study examined the impact of an artificial intelligence skill-up educational programme on mitigating youth unemployment for community development in Imo State. The study adopted a descriptive survey design, with a population of 6700 youth participants and a sample size of 469 selected using a proportionate sampling technique. The research instrument was a structured questionnaire titled “Artificial Intelligence Skill-up Educational Programme Questionnaire (AISEPQ)”. Mean, standard deviation, and analysis of variance were used for data analysis. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence has increased youth confidence in competing for digital job opportunities, enabled them to access remote work and other digital employment opportunities more easily, given them a competitive advantage over other job seekers in the digital labour market, improved their chances of securing gainful employment that is directly aligned with the current job demands, and opened up employment opportunities that were previously unavailable. The study concludes that artificial intelligence boosted young people's confidence in pursuing digital job opportunities, facilitated their access to remote work and other digital employment options. It recommends that the Federal Ministry of Youth Development (FMYD), in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Education (FME), sufficiently allocate resources for the transition period of the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions so that young people can meet the demands of a knowledge-based economy.

items.title: Impact of Expertise and Trust on AI-assisted Work
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents promise to extend what users can accomplish beyond their existing expertise, but they also raise the risk of producing plausible-looking work that users may struggle to evaluate. We ask how task-relevant expertise and trust in AI shape agent-assisted work. To isolate these factors, we conduct a think-aloud study in which 20 professionals with varying data-science expertise use the same agentic tool to complete the same data-science hiring assessment, used at a major U.S. company. We find that surface productivity can come at the expense of understanding: participants who delegated more completed more of the task, but were also more likely to produce invalid solutions. Experts more often resisted this tradeoff, sacrificing completion to decompose the task and scrutinize agent outputs. Our findings call for evaluating agentic assistance not only by how much it accomplishes, but by whether users remain able to evaluate the work they produce.

items.title: Intellectual Property Protection of Purely AI-Generated Content: Rethinking Authorship, Inventorship, and the Case for International Standards
items.abstract: The rapid growth of generative and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems has unsettled the traditionally anthropocentric foundations of intellectual property (IP) law. This article examines the extent to which existing intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks, namely copyright, patent, and industrial design law, can accommodate works, inventions, and designs that are created exclusively by AI systems without direct human intervention. Adopting a doctrinal legal research methodology, the article reviews primary legal materials, including statutes, international conventions, and case law from several jurisdictions, alongside secondary scholarly literature, to assess how the requirements of authorship, inventorship, originality, and moral rights have been interpreted in the context of purely AI-generated content. The discussion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of jurisdictional responses in the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. The central argument advanced is that traditional IPR laws were designed around human creativity and therefore struggle to extend coverage to autonomously generated content. While a few jurisdictions have experimented with liberal judicial interpretation or sui generis protection, these efforts remain fragmented, inconsistent, and largely reactive rather than systematic. The article concludes that an internationally coordinated framework, whether through reform of existing treaties or the negotiation of a dedicated IP-AI instrument, is necessary to balance innovation incentives, economic interests, and the public interest in access to AI-generated content.

items.title: Knowledge Evolution and Paradigm-Level Change in AI-in-Education Research: A Scientometric Mapping and Critical Review (2015–2025)
items.abstract: Bibliometric commentary increasingly frames the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a paradigm shift in AI-in-education (AIED) research, yet rarely distinguishes publication growth from genuine reconfiguration of the knowledge base or of teacher–learner roles. This study maps knowledge evolution in AIED from 2015 to 2025 by integrating four analytical strands across Web of Science and Scopus: scientometric mapping (including keyword and reference bursts and co-citation analysis), structural topic modeling (STM), design-weighted coding of full texts, and triangulation across these strands. Two transition windows emerged. The weaker 2019–2020 window (Jensen–Shannon divergence, JSD = 0.058; retained under the permutation rule but not under a stricter interval-based rule) reflects a research-front transition toward learning analytics and prediction, accompanied by knowledge-base reconfiguration but no detectable change in teacher–learner roles. The 2022–2023 window (JSD = 0.187, the period maximum) coincides with the generative-AI surge and couples a newly formed co-citation community with a topic-specific rise in coagency whose direction is clear but whose magnitude is imprecisely estimated. Because these effects concentrate in 36.6% of the weighted corpus and recent citations remain right-censored, we classify the change, under our pre-specified labeling scheme, as localized paradigm-level reconfiguration rather than a field-level paradigm shift. The label is an operational classification within that scheme, not an independent determination that a paradigm shift has occurred.

items.title: Modeling Cooperation as Information Flow: Ripple Structures and Behavioral Digital Twins
items.abstract: Recent advances in articial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models, havesignicantly improved performance in language understanding, vision, and reasoning. How-ever, a fundamental limitation remains: current AI systems still lack an explicit under-standing of the logical structure by which humans make decisions within specic situationsand relationships. This limitation is not merely a shortage of intelligence, but a missinglayer of context-dependent decision logic. This study proposes a theoretical framework andmethodological protocol that redenes human cooperation as an observable information owrather than a psychological or moral phenomenon. We model cooperative propagation asRipple structures, which are directional causal chains of actions in which A helps B and B inturn helps C, and we introduce the concept of a Behavioral Digital Twin, dened as a map-ping of decision logic derived from situation, relationships, and action history. We furtherpresent a non-interventional observational protocol for capturing naturally occurring coop-erative behaviors through naturalistic observation environments, and outline a validationframework for future empirical work. All behavioral events remain voluntary; the proto-col introduces observation infrastructure without prescribing or incentivizing actions. Allgures and examples in this manuscript are conceptual illustrations intended to clarify the-oretical constructs. This work aims to provide a foundational layer connecting AI research,social systems research, and Web3 governance.

items.title: Motivation And Performance In Project-Based Organizations: Evidence From Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between motivation and performance in project-based organizations in Abia State, Nigeria.Specifically, it investigated the influence of intrinsic motivation on individual performance; the effect of extrinsic motivational factors on team performance; the mediating roles of knowledge sharing and collaborative behaviors in the motivation-innovation performance relationship; and the moderating role of corporate culture in the motivation-project performance relationship.The study adopted a pragmatist philosophical position and a convergent parallel mixed-methods design.Quantitative data were obtained through a structured questionnaire from 402 valid respondents out of 420 distributed questionnaires, representing a 95.7% response rate, while qualitative evidence was obtained from 22 semi-structured interviews.Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression, Hayes PROCESS mediation and moderation procedures, and thematic analysis.Results showed that intrinsic motivation strongly predicted individual performance (β = 0.634, R² = 0.402, p < 0.001), while extrinsic motivation significantly predicted team performance (β = 0.492, R² = 0.242, p < 0.001).Knowledge sharing and collaborative behaviors significantly mediated motivation and innovation performance, with indirect effects of 0.152 and 0.127, respectively.Corporate culture significantly moderated the motivation-project performance relationship (interaction B = 0.192, p < 0.001), with the model explaining 42.0% of variance.The findings indicate that project-based organizations should combine intrinsic and extrinsic motivational practices with supportive cultural conditions and structured knowledge-sharing mechanisms.

items.title: Multimodal Trust Assessment in Human–AI Shared Control Systems
items.abstract: Trust plays an important role in human–AI shared-control systems, yet it is difficult to assess from a single observable signal. This study proposes an event-centered multimodal framework for assessing situational trust by integrating contextual, behavioral, affective, and individual features surrounding critical human–AI interaction events. A controlled autonomous-driving experiment was conducted with 15 participants under high- and low-reliability conditions, yielding 117 valid event-level observations with retrospective trust ratings. The results showed substantial differences in reported trust between reliability conditions and across failure types, while facial and failure-related contextual indicators were among the more informative variables. However, the highly imbalanced trust classes, particularly the limited number of high-trust observations, constrained reliable classification of individual trust levels. The findings only provide preliminary evidence that event-level multimodal observations can characterize information associated with reported situational trust, while also demonstrating the challenges of cross-user trust estimation under limited and imbalanced data. Therefore, the study serves as a methodological and empirical starting point for developing more robust multimodal trust assessment approaches, rather than as a validation of a generalized real-time trust prediction system.

items.title: NAVIGATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND RELIGIOUS AUTHORITY IN NIGERIA: RECONFIGURING RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, LEADERSHIP AND TRUST IN THE DIGITAL AGE
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of religious education, communication, research and everyday faith practices. Believers can now use generative AI to explain sacred texts, compare interpretations, prepare devotional materials and seek answers to religious questions without first consulting a recognised religious leader. This development raises an important question for Nigeria: how is religious authority changing when access to religious information is no longer controlled mainly by clergy, scholars and religious institutions? This paper examines the relationship between AI and religious authority in Nigeria, focusing on religious knowledge, leadership and trust. Using a conceptual and interpretive methodology, it synthesises scholarship on religious authority, digital religion, AI ethics and Nigerian religious experience. It argues that AI is not simply replacing religious authorities; rather, it is reconfiguring the conditions under which authority is produced, accessed, evaluated and trusted. Nigerian digital-religion research shows that digital infrastructures can create new forms of religious influence and authority, while recent AI scholarship highlights concerns about accuracy, privacy, bias and human accountability. The paper proposes a Responsible Religious AI Engagement Framework based on human accountability, verification, contextual sensitivity, confidentiality and formation. It concludes that Nigerian religious institutions should neither reject AI nor surrender religious judgment to it. AI should remain an assistive instrument while theological discernment, pastoral responsibility, communal recognition and human dignity remain central to religious leadership.

items.title: Observing passenger behavior and motion sickness development in autonomous vehicles – A driving study on public roads
items.abstract: Highly automated vehicles (HAV) enable passengers to engage in non-driving related activities (NDRA), which are a known factor for increasing motion sickness (MS). Surveys show that NDRAs will not significantly change compared to manual driving, but they lack experiential insight. The study investigated NDRAs in automated versus manual driving, the influence of MS susceptibility, and the effect of self-chosen NDRAs on MS. In the online survey (N = 611), 52% of participants reported avoiding NDRAs to prevent MS. NDRA frequency showed a small but significant effect of MS susceptibility on certain NDRA choices. Within the on-road study (N = 44), most participants (86%) chose reading as NDRA, either on a smartphone or in a book. Video recordings showed smartphones and tablets as the most frequently used devices. No influence of MS susceptibility on NDRA choice was observed in automated driving. Most participants reported they were reading during MS occurrence.

items.title: Optimising Automotive Wiring Harness Production Through Collaborative Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Twins: A Structured Narrative Review
items.abstract: Automotive wiring harnesses are safety-critical subassemblies whose complexity grows with driver-assistance systems, electrification, and connectivity, while pre-assembly and final assembly remain predominantly manual. This structured narrative review examines how collaborative robots (cobots), AI-based perception and planning, and Digital Twins (DTs) support harness production, with deformable-linear-object (DLO) perception and manipulation treated as a cross-cutting harness-specific domain. A database search (2015–early 2026) yielded 64 studies; citation tracking and a targeted update to 30 August 2026 added 19, giving an evidence base of 83 studies. Reported outcomes were separated into algorithm, task, operator, and system levels, and maturity was graded with explicit, review-specific Technology Readiness Level (TRL) criteria. Most evidence is at the algorithm, task, or operator level. Harness-specific cobot workstations reach industrially relevant prototype validation for single operations—for example, cobot-assisted taping with an approximately 50% reduction in ergonomic risk scores and a 12% shorter cycle—whereas harness-specific perception and DLO manipulation remain mainly at laboratory level. System-level evidence on throughput, changeover, and cost is scarce, and no continuously operating cell integrating the three core domains was identified. Key gaps concern branched DLO modelling, ergonomics-aware task planning, Human Digital Twins, connector design for automation, DT-supported safety verification, digital continuity, and reconfigurable hardware.

items.title: Outcomes-Based Independent Learning Paradigm (OBILP): Effects on Students' Engagement and Performance in Chemistry
items.abstract: This study investigated the effects of the Outcomes-Based Independent Learning Paradigm (OBILP) on Grade 10 students’ engagement and performance in chemistry, focusing on the domains of gas laws, biomolecules, and chemical equations and reactions. An Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods design was employed. The quantitative phase utilized a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design involving Grade 10 students from Bacayawan National High School during the school year 2022–2023. Results indicated that both control and experimental groups exhibited very high levels of affective engagement and high levels of behavioral and cognitive engagement, with no significant differences across the three components. However, the experimental group achieved significantly higher mean scores (p = 0.010) and mean gain scores (p = 0.035) than the control group. No significant correlation was found between students’ engagement and performance before and after the intervention. The qualitative phase, through interviews and student journal entries, provided explanatory insights into these findings, revealing that OBILP enhanced student engagement and performance, while chemical reactions and equations remained the most challenging topic domain. These results suggest that OBILP has the potential to improve chemistry learning outcomes, although future studies should employ larger samples and broader contexts to strengthen generalizability.

items.title: Parallel science and technology for C2 in the agentic age: from military operations to peaceful sustainability and resiliency
items.abstract: Abstract Command and control (C2) has traditionally been framed as a military problem of sensing, deciding, coordinating, and acting under uncertainty, conflict, and time pressure. In the agentic age, however, this problem is being extended far beyond the battlefield, as human organizations become increasingly embedded in hybrid environments composed of artificial agents, digital twins, social sensing networks, foundation models, autonomous platforms, and cyber–physical–social institutions. This article develops a conceptual framework for parallel science and technology for C2 by revisiting the historical mission of C2 as a quest for certainty under diversity, uncertainty, and complexity (DUC), and by tracing its transformation toward focus, agility, and convergence (FAC). Building on parallel systems, artificial societies, computational experiments, parallel execution (ACP), cyber–physical–social systems (CPSS), C2 management (C2M), planning–readiness–execution–assessment (PREA) loops, social cognition operations, and parallel battlefield intelligence, the article argues that C2 should be reframed as a general science of coordinated adaptation. It further examines emerging agentic societies as a new operating ecology, explains why parallel science and technology are needed, and redefines the mission of future C2 around sustainability and resiliency. Rather than merely accelerating decision cycles or optimizing combat efficiency, parallel C2 aims to support anticipation, adaptation, trust, recovery, and responsible human agency across both military and civilian domains, thereby transforming command and control from post-hoc operational control into a science of sustainable and resilient coordination in the agentic age.

items.abstract: This thesis investigates the structured integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools within higher pedagogical education under specialty 13.00.01. As educational paradigms shift globally towards digital environments, future educators must develop comprehensive digital-pedagogical competencies. The study highlights the key technical, methodological, and psychological conditions necessary to successfully adapt generative AI systems like large language models and smart tutoring agents in training workflows. Ultimately, the paper proposes a cohesive pedagogical framework aimed at boosting critical thinking and lesson planning efficiency among upcoming school teachers.

items.title: Pedagogical Foundations of Active Learning: Rethinking Teaching Approaches for the Next Generation of Educators
items.abstract: Active learning is widely promoted to enhance learner participation and meaningful learning, yet its conceptualization remains fragmented across instructional techniques, engagement processes, teacher roles, and emerging technological contexts. This conceptual article reconsiders active learning as a coherent pedagogical orientation and develops an integrative account of its pedagogical foundations for the next generation of educators. Drawing on a thematic synthesis of relevant literature, the article identifies interconnected dimensions comprising pedagogical purpose, meaningful learning activity, cognitive engagement, teacher facilitation, learner agency, feedback, relational conditions, and digital/AI environments. The synthesis positions cognitive engagement as a central mechanism through which purposeful activities contribute to meaningful learning, while teacher facilitation and learning conditions sustain this process. The resulting framework conceptualizes active learning as a dynamic, interdependent, and recursive pedagogical system, rather than a linear sequence or collection of techniques. Digital and AI technologies are positioned as contextual pedagogical affordances whose value depends on purposeful integration and critical use. The framework repositions teachers as pedagogical designers and facilitators who orchestrate learning conditions while sustaining learner agency. This conceptualization provides a coherent foundation for understanding active learning and preparing educators to design meaningful, learner-centered environments responsive to contemporary educational demands.

items.title: Safety concepts through a memetic lens
items.abstract: Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice.

items.title: Scaffold or Cognitive Crutch? A Two-Level Meta-Analysis of AI Scaffolding Effects on Achievement and Self-Regulated Learning in STEM Education
items.abstract: Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) now mediates much of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning, yet adoption has outpaced theory. The tension is whether AI scaffolding relieves cognitive burden or performs the self-regulatory work autonomy requires, and implementation varies too widely for a single average to describe. Objectives. This review estimates the pooled effect of AI scaffolding on STEM achievement and self-regulated learning, tests whether technological paradigm moderates that effect, and asks whether the literature can evaluate learning after support is withdrawn. Methods. Under PRISMA 2020, four platforms searched in October 2026 (spanning 2021–2026) yielded 21,819 records; 13,786 unique records were dual-screened into an 83-record corpus, then 41 extracted cohorts. Each contributes one harmonised contrast (k = 29; N = 3,709), so within-study dependence is structurally absent. Effects were pooled by two-level random-effects meta-analysis fitted with restricted maximum likelihood and Knapp–Hartung adjustment. Results. The pooled effect was Hedges g = 0.8045 (95% CI [0.5469, 1.0621]), with τ² = 0.4410 and I² = 92.78%. The 95% prediction interval [−0.5846, 2.1936] spans zero, and no moderator reached significance. Notably, 27 of 29 cohorts (93.1%) never withdrew support, and none measured unassisted performance after removal. Conclusions. AI scaffolding yields a large but implementation-dependent gain, consistent with extraneous-load offloading rather than cognitive substitution. The decisive finding is the shape of the evidence base: the field measured a human-AI system in assembly and stayed silent on the competence of the human alone. We name this evidentiary void the Autonomy Gap. items.title: Semantic Privilege Collapse: Trust Boundaries and Execution-Level Authorization in Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: Large language model agents operating within tool-enabled pipelines create opportunities for untrusted content to influence consequential actions. This note introduces semantic privilege collapse as an architectural failure condition in which task data or insufficiently authorized instructions are promoted into effective action authority through model interpretation. The term does not claim discovery of a wholly new vulnerability: it synthesizes the confused-deputy problem, prompt-injection risks, capability-oriented control, and modern agentic authorization requirements. Drawing on OWASP’s 2025 LLM Top 10, OWASP agent-security guidance, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Simon Willison’s Dual LLM pattern, and Google DeepMind’s CaMeL research, the note distinguishes behavioral resistance to prompt injection from independently enforced execution authorization. It further distinguishes a principal’s standing permissions from task-specific authority and action-specific approval. The central argument is that semantic interpretation is not authorization evidence: protected operations require complete mediation through controls that validate identity, scope, policy, and required approvals independently of model-generated assertions. The analysis recognizes that malicious actions can remain policy-permitted when enforced policies are broader than the intended task. A reference security stack, properties of effective execution authorization, and proposed evaluation criteria are held in a restricted companion edition.

items.title: Simulating Employment Displacement under Partial, Advanced and Near-Full AI and Automation Deployment in Bangladesh's Ready-Made Garment Factories: A Process-Level Model
items.abstract: This paper presents a process-level simulation of employment impacts from artificial intelligence and automation in Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) sector. Using a representative 1,500-worker factory calibrated to recent empirical evidence, three scenarios are modelled: partial automation reflecting current observed trends (approximately 34 per cent reduction), advanced automation combined with AI applications (approximately 58 per cent reduction), and a near-full theoretical maximum (approximately 75 per cent reduction). Results indicate that helpers and lower-skilled operators bear the largest absolute and relative losses, with women accounting for roughly two-thirds of displaced workers across scenarios. Scaling the advanced scenario to sector level produces job losses on the order of 2.3 million, consistent in magnitude with independent forward projections. Technical constraints on fully autonomous sewing of complex garments, combined with potential output growth and new technical roles, moderate absolute employment decline. The findings underscore the urgency of just-transition policies, targeted reskilling, and product upgrading for Bangladesh's largest export industry. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. items.title: Structural Modeling of Cognitive Load Reduction in ChatGPT-Supported Learning
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, is transforming computer-assisted learning and teaching in higher education. This study investigates how ChatGPT can support learning by reducing cognitive load, with particular emphasis on the roles of user technological confidence and affective trust in artificial intelligence within the framework of Cognitive Load Theory. The study employs quantitative analysis based on data from 12,085 respondents across 135 countries, including undergraduate and postgraduate students and academic researchers. The data were analyzed using a PLS-SEM approach implemented in SmartPLS 4.0 with bootstrapping procedures. The results indicate that ChatGPT use is associated with reduced cognitive load and increased user technological confidence. User technological confidence mediates this relationship, while affective trust in AI acts as a moderating factor. A constraining effect was observed, whereby very high levels of trust in AI are associated with more passive interaction with the technology, weakening the overall effect of cognitive load reduction. These findings contribute to a better understanding of how large language models can be effectively and responsibly integrated into higher education, demonstrating that successful human–AI collaboration depends not only on the availability of AI tools but also on fostering appropriate technological confidence and balanced trust to achieve meaningful learning outcomes.

items.title: Sustainable AI Governance: A Theoretical Framework for Legal Compliance and Environmental Accountability A Systematic Conceptual Review
items.abstract: The fast increase in artificial intelligence (AI) in vital points in society has created significant governance issues at the interface of environmental sustainability and legal responsibility. Although there is a rich literature on AI ethics, technical safety, and standalone regulatory compliance, a cohesive theoretical framework that encompasses both legal compliance and environmental responsibility conditions under one governance framework have not existed yet, seemingly conspicuously in the literature. The review thus poses the question of how legal compliance requirements and environmental accountability requirements for AI systems can be incorporated in one, theoretically coherent governance architecture, and what are the structural gaps in existing regulatory instruments in this context? This gap is filled in this paper, by introducing the Sustainable AI Governance Framework (SAGF) a conceptual model, three pillars in theory which integrates regulatory coherence, environmental accountability and legal compliance architecture. A systematic conceptual review of studies published in the period 2021–2025 and indexed in Scopus, WoS and PubMed (search on 3–10 March 2026) was carried out after PRISMA 2020. For empirical studies, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool was used to assess the quality of the studies and for doctrinal and conceptual studies, a five-item checklist was used. To develop the SAGF, 58 articles in sustainability science, environmental law, governance theory and AI regulation were selected fulfilling the inclusion criteria. The article outlines seven key global regulatory tools, seven research gaps (six corpus-derived and one framework-level), and presents a policy roadmap plan that includes mandatory carbon disclosures by AI, legal harmonization across jurisdictions, and tiered organizational standards of compliance. The results have shown that current regulatory frameworks are methodically ineffective in uniting environmental and legal aspects of AI regulation and expose structural gaps, which are inadequately addressed by technical norms and soft-law tools. The paper adds a theoretically sound and practically feasible model to help legislators, regulatory bodies, AI creators, and legal professionals negotiating the twin demands of both sustainable and legally responsible AI use on a globally scale.

items.title: Sustaining Safe Harbors: The Mediating Roles of SARC and Safety Culture in the Relationship Between OHSMS and Safety Performance in the Port Industry: A Case of Korea
items.abstract: The sustainability of global maritime supply chains ultimately depends on the safety of frontline port workers, yet high-risk, multi-stakeholder port operations continue to face persistent occupational hazards that threaten this goal. Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems (OHSMS) serve as a core governance tool for sustainable safety management, but their effectiveness depends not on formal existence alone, but on workers’ cognitive recognition and cultural internalization, particularly under South Korea’s Serious Accidents Punishment Act. This study examined how OHSMS perception is related to safety performance (SP) among port workers, testing the parallel and serial mediating roles of Serious Accident Response Capability (SARC) and Safety Culture (SC) as pathways toward socially sustainable safety outcomes. Cross-sectional survey data from 432 South Korean port workers were analyzed using structural equation modeling. OHSMS perception was positively associated with both SARC and SC, and SC showed the strongest direct association with SP. In the main model, the direct paths from OHSMS and SARC to SP were non-significant, consistent with indirect-only mediation through SC, and the serial pathway (OHSMS → SARC → SC → SP) was significant; however, the SARC → SP path became significant in a common method sensitivity analysis. These cross-sectional results represent associations rather than causal effects. The findings suggest that safety performance in the port sector is associated less with formal regulatory compliance alone than with the internalization of safety practices in a shared safety culture, which is relevant to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being).

items.title: Talent Intelligence dalam Organisasi Modern: Integrasi Data, Teknologi, dan Pengembangan Talenta
items.abstract: The growth of digital technology and artificial intelligence has pushed companies to handle their employees in a more adaptable and data-based way. Talent Intelligence has become a way to combine worker data, technology, analysis, and people factors to help make better decisions in human resources. This study looks at how Talent Intelligence is used in managing people, what role it plays in finding and boosting employee skills, how technology that uses data affects this process, and what things help or stop organizations from using it effectively today. This study uses a Systematic Literature Review method, which includes steps like searching for sources, screening them, selecting the most relevant ones, and then analyzing the content to find themes and patterns. The results show that Talent Intelligence helps companies find out what each person is good at, understand their skills, help them grow and stay with the company, and plan for future work needs by using data from employees, analyzing people data, and applying artificial intelligence. How well it works depends on the quality of the data, the ability to analyze it, how ready the organization is for digital tools, the rules in place to manage it, and the role people play in using it. The main difficulties are biased algorithms, keeping personal information safe, and how technology can't fully understand human feelings and situations. Talent Intelligence connects technology with talent growth to make organizations more flexible and prepared.

items.title: The Architectural Framework of Agentic AI 2.0
items.abstract: Maintaining coherent agentic work becomes an architectural challenge as information, participants, commitments, execution components, and operating conditions change. This paper proposes Agentic AI 2.0, a system-level architectural framework that integrates established concepts to organize ongoing goal-directed work in foundation-model-based systems. Six constitutive properties characterize this organization: Maintained Process State, Collective Coordination, Shared Operational Knowledge, Governed and Grounded Action, Computational Continuity, and Feedback-Driven Adaptation. The framework connects these properties to role-bearing agents, shared operational objects, interface contracts, and interacting execution, coordination, and adaptation loops. A composition guard specifies how local acceptance decisions connect across operational boundaries, while a criterion-level codebook supports configuration-specific assessment from explicit evidence. We examine the framework through a constructed production-order trace, disruption and handoff branches, counterexamples, and static source profiles of three application configurations and one infrastructure boundary case. The analyses distinguish local feasibility from joint commitments, effect reconciliation from execution-right control, and retained skill versions from governed activation and reuse. They also separate scoped negative evidence from unresolved evidence when diagnosing architectural relationships. Candidate evaluation and later reuse remain conditional in the worked example. Prospective profiles for enterprise productivity, adaptive manufacturing, and distributed mobility identify domain-specific evidence needs and evaluation priorities. The contribution is a traceable basis for architectural analysis, comparison, and design. Independent assessor studies, comparative diagnosis, and controlled and longitudinal implementation studies are needed to establish its practical value and the relationship between architectural choices, operational outcomes, and cost.

items.title: The Extractive Imperative Thesis in AI: Instrumental Training via Soft Hacking for Adversarial Scenario Harvesting in Real Incidents
items.abstract: This working paper poses a methodological alternative to the anthropomorphicnarrative of 'rogue machines' in Artificial Intelligence safety and alignment. It examines the possibility that certain training and evaluation environments, by combining operational restriction conditions with rigid optimization goals, induce secondary rule evasion behaviors ('soft hacking'). Furthermore, it is postulated that the systematic harvesting of these adversarial scenarios could serve to equip second-generation safety monitors with long-range trajectory prediction capabilities and complex cognitive precursor detection, rather than relying solely on the reactive analysis of isolated actions. This paper formalizes this line of research by defining the concept of the extractive imperative as an analytical risk hypothesis, structuring layers of empirical evidence, establishing rigorous operational definitions, and proposing a replicable experimental protocol alongside explicit refutation criteria. Additionally, the concept of liability laundering is addressed as a legal-organizational risk hypothesis, explicitly separating technical design, economic incentives, internal knowledge, intent, and legal liability.

items.title: The HCI-H Model: Development of a Context-Sensitive Mathematical Framework for Prospective Healthcare Procedure Risk Assessment and Preventive Decision Support
items.abstract: This project proposes the development of the HCI-H Model, a multidimensional mathematical framework designed to assess the risk of harm associated with healthcare procedures according to local clinical and organizational conditions. The model integrates human factors, organizational risks, punitive culture, professional hierarchy, humanization of care, patient vulnerability, artificial intelligence-related risks, clinical decision-making, and the unjustified dismissal of safety warnings. Risk management and organizational resilience are incorporated as protective factors. The proposed mathematical equation aims to generate a relative risk score that may support the prospective identification of unsafe conditions and inform decisions regarding additional preventive measures, supervision, and safety barriers. This research protocol presents the theoretical foundations, mathematical formulation, and proposed methods for examining the model's consistency, sensitivity, and applicability across healthcare settings. The HCI-H Model is currently a theoretical framework under development. Its mathematical assumptions, predictive performance, and clinical utility require further empirical validation before implementation as a clinical decision-support tool.

items.title: The impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical decision-making and patient safety: A narrative review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), in the form of large language models (LLMs), has entered clinical practice faster than the evidence on how it changes clinical decisions could be produced. The relevant question is therefore no longer whether these models hold medical knowledge, but whether their use makes clinicians' decisions better and patients' care safer. This narrative review examines the evidence on the impact of generative AI on clinical decision-making and patient safety. In evaluations of encoded knowledge, a medically aligned model gave answers that agreed with scientific consensus in 92.6% of cases, against 92.9% for clinicians. In diagnostic reasoning, a model optimized for diagnosis outperformed unassisted clinicians on challenging cases and improved the differential diagnoses of the clinicians who used it, whereas a randomized trial of a general-purpose chatbot found no significant improvement in physicians' diagnostic reasoning, although the model alone outperformed both physician groups. In management reasoning, physicians assisted by GPT-4 scored 6.5 percentage points higher than those using conventional resources. When tested on real patient data in a simulated clinical workflow, however, LLMs diagnosed less accurately than physicians, did not follow guidelines and were sensitive to the order and quantity of information. The safety literature identifies four recurrent hazards: fabricated content, with hallucination rates of 50% to 82% when prompts contained a false clinical detail; misjudgement of clinical acuity, with drafted patient messages judged to pose a risk of severe harm in 7.1% of assessments; automation bias, by which clinicians adopt the model's assessment in place of their own; and the reproduction of racial and gender stereotypes. Only about 5% of published evaluations used real patient care data. Taken together, the evidence supports generative AI as a supervised aid to clinical reasoning rather than as an autonomous decision-maker, and indicates that its safety depends as much on the design of the human–AI interaction as on the accuracy of the model. Practical safeguards for clinical use are also reviewed.

items.title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN HUMAN COGNITION, SPEECH PERCEPTION, AND AI TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the ways in which language is generated, processed, interpreted, and used in educational communication. This article examines human speech and language perception from a psycholinguistic perspective, focusing on the cognitive mechanisms underlying speech production, comprehension, contextual interpretation, and meaning construction. It compares major principles of human linguistic activity with the text-generation capabilities of large language models and discusses the implications of AI-assisted communication for higher education. Particular attention is given to critical thinking, independent writing, cognitive engagement, linguistic competence, and academic integrity. The study employs a theoretical and analytical methodology based on established psycholinguistic theories and international guidance on generative AI in education. It argues that AI-generated linguistic output should not automatically be equated with human understanding and that educational applications should be designed to support rather than replace learners' cognitive and communicative activities.

items.title: THE ROLE OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN ENSURING RAILWAY TRANSPORT SAFETY
items.abstract: The rapid integration of digital technologies—encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital Twins (DT), and the Internet of Things (IoT)-is fundamentally transforming railway transport safety. This paper presents a critical scientific literature review of recent peer-reviewed advancements in digital railway safety systems, evaluating their operational efficacy, implementation challenges, and theoretical boundaries. The review synthesizes findings on AI-driven predictive maintenance, which transitions railways from reactive troubleshooting to continuous condition-based monitoring, alongside the use of Digital Twins for risk-free virtual simulations. Furthermore, the convergence of Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) in intelligent signalling systems, such as the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS), is examined through the lens of emerging cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Despite significant technological maturation, a critical research gap persists regarding the formal regulatory certification of probabilistic machine learning algorithms for high Safety Integrity Level (SIL) applications. The study concludes that while digital technologies dramatically enhance anomaly detection and system resilience, their integration into autonomous, safety-critical environments relies heavily on the future development of Explainable AI (XAI) validation frameworks and holistic IT-OT cybersecurity models.

items.title: The Third Architecture: Data Capture, Exchange, and Interface Design for the Firm That Executes and Explores
items.abstract: Gabriel runs a firm's AI workforce function. Each quarter, he brings 1,400 pages of reviewer dissent records to a governance session that must answer two questions: where did AI output fail, and where did the firm's methods fail the client? The first question produces decisions in the room. The second does not, so it slips to the next quarter and then out of sight. This paper argues that the pattern is the default whenever one body reads one corpus for both signals under time pressure. It describes the operational layer beneath two earlier papers in the series, one on mixed human-AI delivery and one on sustaining exploration in a codified firm. The layer has four requirements: records produced as a byproduct of work already under way; insight that crosses jurisdictional borders when client data cannot; interfaces that add no documentation load; and a way to tell an accurate corpus from a politically curated one, a risk that is highest in high power-distance cultures. Mechanisms include embedded review capture, a Pattern Contribution Addendum for client consent, a session design that gives methodology items their own closure, and a three-phase minimum viable deployment. Most of them work without the parent architectures. Working paper, not peer-reviewed. The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not represent the position of his employer or any of its member firms.

items.title: The Threat of AI Automation on Employment Termination: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) across industries has intensified concerns regarding labor substitution, yet scholarly literature on AI-driven employment termination remains fragmented. This study systematically identifies displacement mechanisms, maps vulnerable sectors and workforce categories, and synthesizes mitigation strategies. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted via Google Scholar across three search sessions, yielding 25 eligible peer-reviewed articles (2016–2026) from 520 initial records. Data were analyzed using thematic synthesis complemented by keyword co-occurrence bibliometric mapping in VOSviewer. Results indicate four interrelated displacement patterns: hierarchical task substitution, skill degradation and labor market polarization, acceleration coinciding with generative AI, and opaque algorithmic layoff practices. Service, information technology, and labor-intensive sectors are identified as most vulnerable, with middle-skilled workers experiencing the greatest structural pressure. Effective mitigation requires a simultaneous three-pillar approach: competency-based reskilling, algorithmic accountability regulation, and collaborative labor union engagement, with proactive timing highlighted as critical. These findings offer a synthesized evidence base for policymakers and organizations navigating an AI-augmented labor market. Given that only one reviewed study directly examined Indonesia, these findings serve as contextual implications rather than direct empirical assertions, underscoring the necessity for future primary research in developing national contexts.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DEVELOPING RUBRICS FOR STUDENT ASSESSMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping assessment practices in higher education and is creating new opportunities for the design of transparent, scalable, and learning-oriented assessment instruments. This conceptual research article examines how artificial intelligence can support the development of analytic rubrics while preserving teacher agency and assessment validity. The study uses an integrative literature review and design-oriented conceptual analysis of research on scoring rubrics, AI-supported assessment, generative AI, and international guidance for responsible AI in education. Rather than treating AI as an autonomous grader, the article conceptualizes AI as a rubric-design assistant operating within a human-in-the-loop model. The proposed framework comprises seven stages: learning-outcome analysis, task analysis, AI-assisted criterion generation, descriptor generation, expert validation, pilot calibration, and iterative refinement. The analysis identifies four principal opportunities: reducing rubric-development workload, improving criterion coverage, facilitating differentiated descriptors, and supporting alignment between learning outcomes and assessment tasks. At the same time, the study identifies significant risks, including generic descriptors, construct underrepresentation, bias, over-reliance on AI-generated language, and inappropriate transfer from rubric generation to autonomous grading. Recent evidence suggests that supervised AI-rubric systems can achieve useful levels of consistency in particular contexts, while broader evidence on AI-based grading remains mixed and context dependent. The article therefore argues that the educational value of AI lies not in replacing professional assessment judgment but in augmenting teachers' capacity to design, test, and refine assessment instruments. The proposed framework provides a practical and theoretically grounded basis for responsible AI-assisted rubric development in higher education.

items.title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
items.abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

items.title: Traversing the Relationship Between Student Engagement and Science Achievement: Sigla Program in Junior Highschool
items.abstract: This research investigated the relationship between student engagement and academic achievement within the context of the S.I.G.L.A. (Science Innovations for Genuinely Localized Action) Program. The research aimed to determine how localized instructional interventions influence the behavioral, emotional, and cognitive involvement of learners and their subsequent mastery of Science competencies in rural secondary schools. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed to analyze the dynamics between engagement dimensions and academic outcomes. The respondents of the study included a total of 110 respondents from select National High Schools in the District of Villaba, Leyte, namely Villaba National Comprehensive High School, Cahigan National High School, and Sambulawan National High School. The teacher-respondent profile (n=5) consisted of licensed professional educators, primarily aged 26–45, with a balanced gender distribution and active involvement in graduate studies. The student-respondent profile (n=105) comprised Junior High School learners, predominantly aged 13–16, coming from low-income households with a monthly family income typically below ₱10,000. Results indicated that the S.I.G.L.A. Program is perceived as "Highly Positive" (3.70) by stakeholders, with its gamified and localized activity exemplars receiving the highest approval. Student engagement was found to be generally high (3.23), characterized by "Very High" Emotional Engagement but relatively lower Cognitive Engagement. In terms of academic performance, the respondents demonstrated a Satisfactory level of Science achievement (81.76); however, competency-based assessments highlighted a significant struggle in Higher-Order Thinking Skills (HOTS), particularly in analyzing and synthesizing (77.50%). Correlational analysis revealed a significant relationship between engagement levels and Science achievement, though this relationship is hindered by a Linguistic Barrier (82.7%) and a Lack of Laboratory Equipment (75.5%). The study concludes that while the S.I.G.L.A. Program effectively captivated students through localized interest, cognitive scaffolding and translanguaging strategies are necessary to translate engagement into mastery. The study recommends the formal adoption of the S.I.G.L.A. Science Enhancement Program to institutionalize community-based inquiry and dismantle the linguistic and resource-based barriers in the District of Villaba.

items.title: Trends in 21st-Century Learning Technology Research: Digital Transformation, AI, and Adaptive Learning
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive learning is reshaping 21st-century education, yet their interrelationships and research trajectories remain fragmented. This study systematically reviews research published from 2020 to 2026 to examine the evolution, dominant and emerging themes, and conceptual relationships across digital transformation, AI, and adaptive learning. Using a systematic literature review with thematic synthesis, relevant studies were analyzed temporally and thematically to identify shifts in research orientation and emerging directions. The findings reveal a progressive transition from technology integration and digital learning environments toward intelligent tutoring, personalization, adaptive learning, and, more recently, generative AI and human–AI collaboration. Conceptually, digital transformation functions as the enabling ecosystem, AI as an intelligent capability, and adaptive learning as a learner-responsive application. Importantly, AI-enabled personalization does not necessarily constitute adaptive learning; meaningful adaptation requires continuous responsiveness to learner performance, needs, feedback, and learning trajectories. The synthesis further indicates that technological advancement alone is insufficient, highlighting teacher agency, learner autonomy, organizational readiness, data governance, and ethical accountability. The study proposes a human-centered and responsible orientation in which AI augments pedagogical judgment rather than displacing it.

items.title: Trust Calibration in Agentic AI Clinical Decision Support: How Autonomy Level and Transparency Mechanism Shape Clinician Reliance
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are rapidly entering healthcare. Unlike static AI, agentic systems exert persistent, goal-directed influence over care trajectories, creating new and largely unstudied challenges for clinician trust and reliance calibration. Drawing on trust calibration theory, human-AI complementarity research, and augmented intelligence literature, this paper develops a model examining how two design dimensions of agentic clinical AI, autonomy level and transparency mechanism, shape clinician trust calibration and downstream outcomes, including decision quality, cognitive load, and error detection. We propose an experiment with clinicians using clinical vignettes across three temporally sequenced decision steps. We contribute: a reconceptualization of trust calibration as a dynamic, temporally extended process; a theorization of autonomy level and transparency as orthogonal design dimensions with interacting effects on calibration; and a falsifiable hypothesis set and an experimental design for validation. The proposed study has the potential to advance theory on human-agentic AI collaboration and inform governance design for high-stakes IS deployments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: Understanding preferences for explainable AI: A study on LIME variations
items.abstract: The current research aims to empirically examine user preferences of four variations of visual explanations from an image classification model. Participants (N = 23) were recruited from a Midwestern university. The study was a within-subjects design in which participants were asked to rate four local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) variations from best to worst in an image classification task across 10 trials. A Friedman's test and a Plackett-Luce analysis were conducted to examine participants' rank-order preferences for the variations, and a linear mixed-effects model on eye-tracking data was used to examine on which variations participants expended the most visual effort. Results reveal that, overall, participants preferred images that were non-obfuscated and spent more time fixating on images that highlighted both positive and negative features compared to positive only features. The findings have implications for interface design, particularly for designers aiming to prioritize human-centered preferences.

items.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
items.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
